subject: microbiology
title: Sandfly Transmission, Trypanosoma cruzi and Chagas Disease

steps.tx: Transmission of visceral leishmaniasis in the Indian subcontinent depends strictly upon the female **Phlebotomus argentipes** sandfly vector. This tiny, hairy nematoceran dipteran measures one point five to three millimetres in length, possesses long slender legs, and rests characteristically with wings held upward in a prominent V-shaped posture. Its short mouthparts limit feeding to painless hopping bites around ankles and mud-plastered dwellings.
steps.say: Small hairy sandflies resting with wings held in a V-shape transmit leishmaniasis during nocturnal feeding.

left.title: Phlebotomus sandfly vector
points: Size: 2 to 3 millimetres, delicate hairy body
Flight: short erratic hopping flights near ground
Resting posture: wings held erect in V-shape
Habitat: cracks in mud walls and damp cattle sheds

right.title: Mosquito vectors (Anopheles / Culex)
points: Size: 4 to 8 millimetres, larger smooth wings
Flight: sustained directional flight across distances
Resting posture: wings folded flat over abdomen
Habitat: open water collections and drainage ditches

steps.tx: In the Americas, zoonotic flagellates belong to the genus Trypanosoma. The protozoan **Trypanosoma cruzi** causes American trypanosomiasis, known universally as Chagas disease, endemic from Mexico through Central and South America. The parasite alternates between circulating C-shaped flagellated trypomastigotes in blood and intracellular round aflagellate amastigotes inside cardiac myocytes, gastrointestinal plexus neurons, and reticuloendothelial cells.
steps.say: Trypanosoma cruzi shifts between circulating blood trypomastigotes and intracellular amastigotes in myocardium.

vis.caption: Comparative morphology showing C-shaped Trypanosoma cruzi trypomastigotes in blood [Credit: CDC, StewardMD cleared]

steps.tx: Transmission of Trypanosoma cruzi is mediated by nocturnal blood-sucking triatomine bugs of the family Reduviidae, popularly termed **kissing bugs** or assassin bugs, including Triatoma infestans and Rhodnius prolixus. Triatomines infest cracks in adobe walls and thatched roofs, emerging at night to bite exposed sleeping faces. The bug defecates metacyclic trypomastigotes onto host skin while feeding, and scratching rubs contaminated feces into the bite wound.
steps.say: Reduviid kissing bugs defecate infectious trypomastigotes while feeding, which scratching rubs into the wound.

nodes.label: Triatomine kissing bug takes nocturnal blood meal on sleeping host
Bug defecates infectious metacyclic trypomastigotes on adjacent skin
Host scratches pruritic site, rubbing feces into bite wound or conjunctiva

steps.tx: When metacyclic trypomastigotes contaminate the ocular conjunctiva or palpebral margins, patients develop **Romaña sign**, the pathognomonic clinical hallmark of acute Chagas disease. It presents as unilateral, painless, brawny periorbital and palpebral oedema accompanied by regional preauricular lymphadenopathy and conjunctivitis. Inoculation through skin produces an erythematous, indurated subcutaneous nodule termed a chagoma.
steps.say: Painless unilateral eyelid swelling and preauricular lymphadenopathy constitute the pathognomonic Romaña sign.

rows: Unilateral painless palpebral oedema with preauricular lymph node
Sinus tachycardia, prolonged PR interval, low ejection fraction
High mortality acute presentation in congenital infection

steps.tx: One eyelid is swollen and painless, and a node sits in front of the same ear, after trypanosomes contaminate the conjunctiva. **Romaña sign** is the hallmark of acute Chagas disease when metacyclic trypomastigotes reach the eye or the lid margin. The oedema is brawny and unilateral, and conjunctivitis accompanies the preauricular node. Entry through skin instead produces a firm red subcutaneous nodule called a chagoma. Painless swelling separates this eye finding from ordinary orbital cellulitis.
steps.say: Romaña sign is painless swelling of one eyelid with conjunctivitis and a node in front of the ear, after the parasite reaches the eye. A skin entry point forms a firm nodule called a chagoma instead.

vis.alt: One side of the face shows painless swelling of the eyelids and a swollen preauricular lymph node.
vis.caption: Unilateral painless periorbital oedema with a node in front of the ear is the Romaña sign of acute Chagas disease. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Following an asymptomatic latent phase lasting decades, thirty percent of chronically infected individuals progress to **Chagas cardiomyopathy**. Intracellular amastigote proliferation combined with autoimmune destruction of cardiac myocytes and conduction fibers induces chronic fibrosing myocarditis. Characteristic features include cardiac enlargement, refractory congestive heart failure, apical left ventricular aneurysm with mural thrombosis, and right bundle branch block.
steps.say: Chronic myocardial fibrosis leads to apical left ventricular aneurysms and right bundle branch block.

left.title: Cardiac manifestations
points: Right bundle branch block and bifascicular block
Malignant ventricular arrhythmias and sudden death

right.title: Digestive manifestations
points: Loss of myenteric Auerbach plexus neurons
Megacolon presenting with severe chronic obstipation
Sigmoid volvulus and secondary intestinal perforation

steps.tx: In the gastrointestinal tract, parasite-mediated destruction of postganglionic parasympathetic neurons in Auerbach's myenteric plexus produces denervation and smooth muscle dilatation, resulting in **megadisease**. Loss of esophageal lower sphincter relaxation mimics primary achalasia, creating mega-oesophagus with progressive dysphagia, regurgitation, and nocturnal aspiration. Destruction of colonic plexuses causes megacolon with intractable constipation, fecaloma impaction, and sigmoid volvulus.
steps.say: Myenteric plexus neuronal loss drives denervation and dilatation, creating mega-oesophagus and megacolon.

rows: Megaureter and secondary urinary tract infections

steps.tx: During the acute phase, direct examination of Giemsa-stained blood films demonstrates typical C-shaped or S-shaped **trypomastigotes** measuring twenty micrometres in length with a central nucleus and a prominent, subterminal posterior kinetoplast. In chronic indeterminate disease where blood parasitaemia is subpatent, historical diagnosis utilized xenodiagnosis, where uninfected laboratory-reared triatomine bugs fed on the patient are dissected weeks later to inspect gut flagellates.
steps.say: Acute infection reveals C-shaped trypomastigotes in blood; xenodiagnosis or serology confirms chronic disease.

nodes.label: Acute phase: identify C-shaped trypomastigotes on peripheral blood film
Chronic phase: perform dual serology (ELISA plus indirect immunofluorescence)
Indeterminate status: perform blood polymerase chain reaction targeting satellite DNA

steps.tx: First-line antiparasitic therapy relies on the nitroheterocyclic agents **benznidazole** or nifurtimox, which generate reactive oxygen radicals that damage trypanosomal nucleic acids. Treatment is highly curative during acute infection, congenital transmission, and early chronic infection in children. In long-standing chronic cardiomyopathy with established organ dilatation, antiparasitic efficacy is markedly reduced, and therapy centers on heart failure management, anticoagulation, and pacemaker implantation.
steps.say: Benznidazole or nifurtimox clears acute parasitaemia but has limited impact once megadisease is established.

rows: High cure rate exceeding 70 to 80 percent
Curative alternative with frequent GI side effects
Halts progression toward cardiac and digestive damage
Standard HF therapy, amiodarone, ICD, transplant
Symptomatic control and prevention of sudden death
